>[!problem] 
>Find the commutator subgroups of the following groups:
>(1) $SL(n,k)$
>(2) $SO(n,k)$
>(3) $Sp(2n,k)$

**Proof:**
**(1)** We have shown in [[Abstract algebra HW1]] that $SL(n,k)$ is generated by elementary matrices with the form $E_{ij}(\alpha)=I+\alpha E_{ij},i\neq j$.
- For $|k|\neq 2$, we have shown in [[Abstract algebra HW4]] that every $E_{ij}(\alpha)$ is a commutator, thus $[SL(n,k),SL(n,k)]=SL(n,k)$.
- For $|k|=2$, i.e. $k=F_{2}$, and $n=2$, we have $SL(2,F_{2})\simeq S_{3}$ (this can be seen by enumerating every element in $SL(2,F_{2})$ and comparing it to $S_{3}$), thus $[SL(2,F_{2}),SL(2,F_{2})]\simeq A_{3}$ (since $[S_{3},S_{3}]=A_{3}$ is shown in [[Abstract algebra HW4]]).
- For $k=F_{2}$ and $n\geq{3}$, we have
$$
E_{ij}(1)=[I+E_{ik},I+E_{kj}+E_{jk}+E_{jj}]
$$
for distinct $i,j,k\in \{ 1,\dots,n \}$. All generators are in $[SL(n,k),SL(n,k)]$, hence $[SL(n,k),SL(n,k)]=SL(n,k)$.

>[!remark] Cartan–Dickson Theorem
>The group $PSL(n, F_{q})$ is simple except for the two small exceptions:
>$$
>PSL(2, F_{2})\simeq S_{3} \quad \text{and} \quad PSL(2, F_{3})\simeq A_{4}.
>$$
>
>Since $SL(n, F_{2})=PSL(n, F_{2})$ is simple and non-abelian for $n\geq 3$, they are all perfect groups.
